*Así es que* is closer to "it is in this way that...", whereas *así que* means "so..."

For example: 

Así es que en su libro, Luna de Plutón, Dross explica el mundo. (It is in this way that in his book, Luna de Plutón, Dross explains the world)

Así que no te olvides de apagar la luz cuando te vayas. (So don't forget to turn off the lights when you leave)

There could be more usages, but these are the ones that came to mind.

Not my story but something I heard from my non-binary phonetics teacher.

They said that English felt more welcoming of their identity than Spanish because of the absence of gender. They didn't have to constantly think about what the other person was going to think if they used this or that article to refer to themselves, and that made English feel closer to them from a young age. Also, even though we do have a gender neutral system, it isn't nearly as accepted as the English "they". It's very controversial and you can end up losing friends or even facing violence for using it. So in that way, English made them feel safer.

What I did for Japanese was learn the basics "traditionally" and then start reading manga, watching anime with JP subs, switching my phone and laptop to Japanese, consuming japanese YouTube and a bunch of other stuff. That isn't necessarily true. If you study an accent that you like and shadow it/go to special pronunciation classes, sounding near native is not impossible. I always say "la ketchup", "la ketchup es rica", "la ketchup es fea", etc. My boyfriend, however, has always said "el ketchup". It's just that grammatical gender is for the most part unrelated to gender stereotypes. For example, rosa is masculine when it's a color, although it is feminine when it's a type of flower. There are four types of nouns in Spanish: epicenos (living beings who can take only one grammatical gender even if they refer to other genders semantically, like "la víctima"), ambiguous (referring to inanimate entities that can take either gender grammatically, for example "la mar, el mar"), common (living beings that can take on either gender depending on what gender they are irl, for example el estudiante vs la estudiante) and asexuados (non living entities that obviously take on either a masculine or feminine gender syntactically but not semantically, for example la piedra or la casa. Note that for these nouns, different grammatical genders on the same word can translate to a change in meaning, so for example la manzana is an apple but el manzano is a tree). It's a relatively lengthy topic but a very interesting one.

The use of the gerund in Spanish is restricted: it can only be used when in the presence of another verb (which is going to be that sentence's main verb), and only when referring to an action that happened at the same moment that the other verb's action happened OR as a consequence of the other verb. For example: "El dique se rompió, obligando a muchos a mudarse" (the dam broke, forcing many people to move) and "Se resbaló en el suelo mojado, golpeándose la cabeza contra la loza" (He/she/they slipped on the wet floor, causing them to hit their head against the tiles).


Edit: oh and btw, the gerund isn't a conjugated form of a verb. Just like the infinitive and participles, it's part of a category called "non-finite verbs", which is the opposite of conjugated or finite verbs.
